extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and early-career fiction writers, especially speculative/genre writers (fantasy, sci-fi, horror)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for genre writers on choosing subjects they want to learn about and using passion-driven research and worldbuilding to create authentic, engaging fiction. Covers what to research, how to research, and how research feeds storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write what you want to know
rubrics_metrics.description: Write what you want to know — pick subjects you want to learn about rather than only writing what you already personally know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hosts quote Laurell: 'Write what you want to know! Dragons, fantastic things! What interests you, what moves you emotionally? Write about that.' The passion for learning will drive you to research and produce details that engage readers. This principle replaces a strict 'write what you know' rule with a motivation-based approach: choose topics that fascinate you so your enthusiasm fuels the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be passionate / choose emotionally compelling interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Select topics that make you happy, fascinate you, or horrify you—things that move you emotionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passion produces deeper, more interesting research and worldbuilding. If you're excited about, for example, how dragons fly or serial killer psychology, you'll study relevant fields more thoroughly and create story elements that 'grab readers because it grabbed you.' This also helps sustain long projects or series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do thorough, multi-source research (start with books)
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin research with books and multiple reputable sources before relying on the internet or experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laurell: 'First step is books and reading about it... Books, not. The. Internet.' Use encyclopedias/dictionaries with good bibliographies as jumping-off points. Multiple sources help verify facts and provide context; do not stop at a single webpage or opinion. For scholarly or complex topics, consult primary texts and standard reference works first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Internet as a jumping-off point, but verify with authoritative sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Wikipedia and web searches to learn keywords and discover authors, but trace claims back to books, academic work, or experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Howard's method: skim Wikipedia for unfamiliar keywords, open linked terms in tabs to build background, then follow bibliography entries to books and authors; find those authors' blogs or publications. The internet is useful for orientation, but it should not be the only research base.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check source credibility and bibliographies
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer sources that include strong bibliographies; distrust sources (including books) that lack references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laurell: choose encyclopedias or dictionaries that provide a good bibliography. If a source doesn't cite its own research, you can't tell how reliable it is—avoid relying on it as an authoritative base for your fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare before interviewing experts—have good, specific questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do background reading before contacting experts so you can ask focused, respectful questions that don't waste their time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laurell: 'Books first... so you have better questions. Don't just go to somebody and say, “Tell me everything you know about X or Y.”' Knowing basics makes expert conversations more efficient and productive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using other fiction as your only research
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely solely on other authors' fiction to learn about a subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laurell warns: 'You can use Internet as a jumping off point... The other thing you cannot do is use other people’s fiction as your only research.' Fiction can inspire, but it often perpetuates inaccuracies; verify with real-world sources when accuracy matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be accurate about technical details to avoid alienating knowledgeable readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Get the right factual and technical details (guns, embalming, horses, etc.) so experts or informed readers won't reject the work's credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dan and Laurell emphasize that detailed, correct facts prevent readers from 'throwing the book across the room.' Accurate research also 'buys goodwill'—readers tolerate imaginative leaps if the grounded details are credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research generates new ideas and enriches worldbuilding
rubrics_metrics.description: Use research not only to check facts but to discover unexpected details that can inspire plot elements, cultural texture, or new directions for your story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Laurell's voodoo research revealed real practices (which lacked ‘shambling dead’) but also suggested other ideas; audience members appreciated respectful research of their faith. Research often produces 'other ideas' that enrich fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple research methods, including hands-on/experiential where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine book/web/archival research with hands-on experiences or observational research when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dan describes hands-on research (mortician/embalming, etc.) and Brandon/Dan mention practical experience. If plausible, doing or observing real procedures, places, or professions can deliver authentic detail that books alone may not convey.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make a list of lifelong interests to find durable creative fuel
rubrics_metrics.description: List things you've loved since childhood or long-term fascinations to identify unique, sustainable subjects to write about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laurell: 'Make a list of the things that interest you... Look at what you've loved since you were small.' These long-term interests are good sources for material you'll enjoy returning to over many books or a series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give yourself 'toys'—elements that keep writing fun
rubrics_metrics.description: Include enough elements, gadgets, creatures, or concepts in your fiction to keep your interest and enjoyment high over many installments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laurell: 'Give yourself enough toys when you’re writing... if I wrote a straight mystery series, I don’t think I’d be in the 20 plus book of the series.' Keeping the work fun for you sustains long-term productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of Dunning–Kruger and know when deeper study is needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that initial surface knowledge can mask ignorance; seek deeper study when you can't tell how little you actually know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Howard explains Dunning–Kruger: you may be 'too dumb to know how dumb you are.' Use bibliographies, experts, and sustained reading to avoid false confidence and mistakes that reveal superficial research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start writing—use prompts or a first sentence to overcome inertia
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin with any sentence or small prompt to get words flowing rather than waiting for the perfect idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laurell's prompt: start with 'I was walking home from work one day.' She emphasizes the 'fish head' analogy: you must write past the initial rough material to discover whether it becomes a story. Don't self-stop before you begin.
